attribution.note: Zitron quotes his own 2024 forecast in his own 2026 post and explicitly re-endorses it as his theory.

semantics.note: Firm 'is going to'/'will' with no deadline. The normalisation keeps the burn-rate cause, the either/or of price rises or onerous new tariffs, and enterprise customers being unable to justify the cost.

contract.note: The plain reading of a causal chain from burn to repricing to enterprise rejection is ordinary and fair. 'Meaningful industry scale' and the thresholds are evaluator choices because the speaker gave none. Treating pre-post changes as background is reasonable.

evidence.note: Anthropic moved enterprise seats to a usage-based plan between Nov 2025 and Feb 2026, before the post. It does not show cash burn as the cause or enterprise rejection.
Cloudera's own commissioned survey ties curtailed use to rising token consumption, not to higher tariffs. As a company disclosure it does not establish the causal chain.

reviews.rationale: Open-ended firm forecast with no deadline. No dated event in the packet establishes the full chain from burn rate to repricing to enterprise rejection. Pricing shifts predate the post or are not shown to stem from cash burn, and the survey covers consumption rather than price. Not yet scoreable.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Present-tense factual claim that each of the five named startups burns $4–5 per $1 of revenue. 'All' applies to each company.

contract.note: The contract picks net cash burn and calendar 2025, but in the same post the speaker says 'spend $3 to $10' per dollar, so gross spend is plausible. The net/gross choice shifts the ratio by $1 and could decide the result. The contract does keep that ambiguity open, so it stays fair.

evidence.note: Cursor's June 2025 funding and ARR disclosure. It gives no cash burn or realised revenue, so no ratio can be computed.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no matched cash-burn and realised-revenue figures for any of the five companies. The only item is a Cursor financing and ARR announcement. The claimed ratio can neither be confirmed nor refuted for any named firm.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the antecedent (death of the AI industry) and marks the Oracle clause as hedged. The firm consequences and the comparison with the 2008 crisis are preserved.

contract.note: The contract requires a verified broad collapse before scoring and treats the Oracle clause as hedged. Its readings of 'cataclysmic', 'hypergrowth' and the crisis scale are ordinary.

evidence.note: Oracle's Oct 2026 press release on an OpenAI partnership. It bears only on the antecedent not having occurred, not on the predicted consequences, so it is context rather than contradiction.

reviews.rationale: Conditional forecast whose antecedent, broad death of the AI industry, has not occurred by the cutoff. Under policy a conditional with an unmet antecedent is not scored. The Oracle release shows only continuing activity.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, citing his own premium model.

semantics.note: Present-tense claim that many projects are unprofitable even with paying customers. The 'based on my model' framing names the source, not a probability hedge. 'Assuming they get built' is rhetorical.

contract.note: Reading 'many' as a substantial, non-isolated set and profitability as full-cost project economics is ordinary and fair. Requiring project-level or reproducible evidence is appropriate.

evidence.note: CoreWeave's company-wide Q4 2025 adjusted margin and net loss, from a company disclosure. Corporate results do not measure project-level profitability or how common unprofitable projects are.
One leased powered-shell project with a projected gross IRR. A single, different-model project cannot show whether 'many' projects are unprofitable.

reviews.rationale: No representative project-level sample and no reproducible model is in the packet. CoreWeave's corporate margins and one profitable-looking powered-shell project neither confirm nor refute that many projects lose money even with paying customers.
